stem: Which expression returns the highest value each node_load1 series reached over the last hour?

options.note: Right. max_over_time returns each series' maximum within the window.
_over_time functions need a range vector. Without [1h] there's no window to take the maximum over.
rate is for counters, and node_load1 is a gauge. It measures change, not a maximum.
That's the value one hour ago, not the maximum during the hour.

explanation: max_over_time(range-vector) returns the maximum value of all float samples in the interval, per series.

stem: Can avg_over_time() be used on a gauge such as process_resident_memory_bytes?

options.text: Yes. _over_time functions summarise samples and don't assume counter behaviour
options.note: Right. Averaging a gauge over a window is a perfectly normal thing to do.

options.text: No, they're for counters only, like rate()
options.note: That restriction applies to rate, irate and increase, not to _over_time functions.

options.text: Only if it's wrapped in rate() first
options.note: rate on a gauge would be wrong. Use avg_over_time directly.
There's no such restriction.

explanation: The _over_time functions aggregate each series of a range vector over time, such as average, min and max. They don't apply counter-reset logic, so they suit gauges.
hint: Is there any counter-reset logic in an average?

options.text: How many samples each api target's up series has in the last hour (roughly the number of scrapes)
options.note: Right. count_over_time counts the samples in the window.

options.text: How many targets are up right now
options.note: That would be a sum of up across targets at one instant, not a count over time.

options.text: The total of all up values
options.note: That's sum_over_time.

options.text: How many times up changed value
options.note: That's changes().

explanation: count_over_time returns the count of all samples in the interval, per series. With up, that roughly equals the number of scrapes.

stem: Which expression gives each series' 95th percentile of node_load1 over the last day?

options.note: Right. The φ comes first, then the range vector.
The argument order is reversed. The scalar φ comes first.
φ is between 0 and 1, so 95th percentile is 0.95.
95% of the maximum isn't the 95th percentile.

explanation: quantile_over_time(scalar, range-vector) returns the φ-quantile (0 ≤ φ ≤ 1) of all float samples in the interval.
hint: Quantiles are written as fractions, and φ goes first.

stem: Samples in a window aren't evenly spaced because a few scrapes were missed. How does avg_over_time weight them?

options.text: Every sample has the same weight, regardless of spacing
options.note: Right. The docs state this explicitly.

options.text: Samples are weighted by the time gap before them
options.note: No time-weighting is applied.

options.text: Missing scrapes are filled with zeros
options.note: Nothing is filled in. Only real samples are averaged.
Uneven spacing is fine. All samples are just weighted equally.

explanation: All values in the interval have the same weight in the aggregation, even if they aren't equally spaced throughout the interval.
hint: The docs make a one-line statement about weights.

stem: You want an alert if a job has reported no my_metric samples at all in the last hour. Which function is designed for this?

options.note: Right. It returns 1 when the range vector has no elements.
If no samples exist there's no series to count, so this returns nothing rather than 0. That's exactly why absent_over_time exists.
A zero rate means the counter didn't grow. It doesn't mean the data is missing.
This returns values when data exists, and nothing when it doesn't. It doesn't produce a 1 for missing data.

explanation: absent_over_time returns an empty vector if the range vector has any elements, and a 1-element vector with value 1 if it has none. It's useful for alerting when no series exist for a period.
hint: Functions that operate on missing data must produce something from nothing.

stem: What does absent(nonexistent{job="myjob"}) return when no such series exist?

options.note: Right. absent tries to derive labels from equality matchers in the selector.
That's what it returns when series do exist.
absent returns 1 for absence, not 0 for presence.
Querying a non-existent metric isn't an error.

explanation: absent returns an empty vector if the input has elements, and a 1-element vector with value 1 if it has none. Labels are derived from the selector where possible.
hint: The docs show this exact example.

stem: Which is a valid subquery that returns the 5-minute rate over the past 30 minutes at 1-minute resolution?

options.note: Right. That's the official example: <instant_query>[<range>:<resolution>].
Without the colon this isn't a subquery, and it's invalid on an expression.
The subquery brackets go after the whole instant query, not inside rate's argument.
This puts the brackets the wrong way round.

explanation: Subquery syntax: <instant_query> '[' <range> ':' [<resolution>] ']'. The result is a range vector.

stem: In max_over_time(rate(x[5m])[1h:]), no resolution is given after the colon. What step is used?

options.note: Right. That's the default resolution for subqueries.

options.text: The scrape interval of the target
options.note: The default is the global evaluation interval, not the scrape interval.
There's no fixed 1s default.
The inner [5m] is the rate window, not the subquery step.

explanation: In a subquery, the resolution is optional. The default is the global evaluation interval.

options.text: max_over_time needs a range vector, but rate() returns an instant vector
options.note: Right. Add a subquery, as in [1h:], to turn the rate into a range vector.

options.text: rate can't be nested inside another function
options.note: Nesting is fine. The issue is the argument type.
_over_time functions work on any series.
The window size isn't the problem.

explanation: _over_time functions take a range vector. rate returns an instant vector, so you need a subquery such as rate(x[5m])[1h:] to produce a range vector from it.
hint: Check the input and output types.

stem: What do the official examples say about subqueries?

options.note: Right. They're expensive. Recording rules are often better for repeated use.

options.text: They're the recommended way to write all alerting rules
options.note: The docs caution against unnecessary use.
Subqueries aren't deprecated.

options.text: They only work in the Graph tab
options.note: They work in any query.

stem: Which function returns the most recent sample of each series within a window, even if that sample is older than the default lookback?

options.note: Right. It returns the most recent sample in the specified interval.
present_over_time returns 1 for any series with samples, not the sample's value.
That counts samples.
That signals missing data.

explanation: last_over_time returns the most recent sample in the specified interval. It's useful when data arrives less often than the 5-minute lookback.
